title: A regular sequence is Koszul-regular
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-module, $r\ge0$, and $f_1,\dots,f_r\in R$ such that for each $i=1,\dots,r$ multiplication by $f_i$ is injective on $M/(f_1,\dots,f_{i-1})M$. Then $f_1,\dots,f_r$ is $M$-Koszul-regular [def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence], i.e. $H_i(K_\bullet(f_1,\dots,f_r)\otimes_RM)=0$ for all $i\neq0$, with $K_\bullet$ the Koszul complex of [def-weil-pbc-koszul-complex]. In particular every $M$-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence] is $M$-Koszul-regular, and every regular sequence in $R$ is Koszul-regular.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma Tag 062F (lemma-regular-koszul-regular, lines 7264-7298; its proof uses Lemma Tag 0629, lemma-cone-koszul, line 6751). Tags verified in tags/tags.

proof.text: Induct on the length $r$. For $r=0$, the Koszul complex tensored with $M$ has $M$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees. For the inductive step put $A_\bullet=K_\bullet(f_1,\dots,f_{r-1})\otimes_RM$. The hypotheses for the prefix are unchanged, so the induction hypothesis gives $H_i(A_\bullet)=0$ for $i>0$. The degree-zero differential has image $(f_1,\dots,f_{r-1})M$, hence $H_0(A_\bullet)=M/(f_1,\dots,f_{r-1})M$. Multiplication by $f_r$ is injective on this quotient by the remaining hypothesis.

source.place: Lemma 062F, lemma-regular-koszul-regular, proof, induction and the short exact sequence, lines 7273-7298

proof.text: Write $E=R^{\oplus(r-1)}$ with basis $e_1,\dots,e_{r-1}$ and let $e_r$ denote the final generator of $E\oplus R$. In every degree the exterior-power basis divides according to whether $e_r$ occurs: $K_n(f_1,\dots,f_r)\otimes_RM\cong A_n\oplus A_{n-1}$, taking $(a,b)$ to $a+e_r\wedge b$. The differential formula of [def-weil-pbc-koszul-complex] gives $D_n(a,b)=(d a+f_r b,-d b)$, because $d(e_r\wedge b)=f_r b-e_r\wedge d b$. Thus this is the mapping-cone description of Stacks Lemma 0629, verified here from the basis and the differential rather than taken as an uncited fact.

source.place: Lemmas 0629 (lemma-cone-koszul, lines 6750-6766) and 0628 (lemma-cone-koszul-abstract, lines 6694-6748), used in the proof of Lemma 062F

proof.text: Let $n>0$ and let $(a,b)\in A_n\oplus A_{n-1}$ be a $D$-cycle. If $n>1$, then $d b=0$ and $H_{n-1}(A)=0$, so write $b=d c$ with $c\in A_n$. If $n=1$, the equation $d a+f_r b=0$ in $A_0=M$ says $f_r[b]=0$ in $H_0(A)$; the injectivity in step 1 gives $[b]=0$, so again $b=d c$, now with $c\in A_1$. In either case subtract $D_{n+1}(0,-c)=(-f_r c,d c)$ from $(a,b)$ to get $(a+f_r c,0)$. Its first coordinate is a $d$-cycle. Since $H_n(A)=0$, choose $e\in A_{n+1}$ with $d e=a+f_r c$; then $(a+f_r c,0)=D_{n+1}(e,0)$. Thus every positive-degree cycle is a boundary, including the edge case $n=1$. By the definition [def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence], the sequence is $M$-Koszul-regular.

proof.text: An $M$-regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence] has exactly the successive injectivity hypothesis already used (and additionally requires a nonzero final quotient); hence it is $M$-Koszul-regular. Taking $M=R$ gives the last assertion for a regular sequence in $R$. For $r=0$ the empty sequence satisfies the first assertion independently of whether the optional nonzero-quotient condition holds.
